objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how a cabin pressurization system holds a cabin altitude, read its gauges, name its failure modes and what decompression does to the people on board, use time of useful consciousness to plan a high-altitude flight, and run the first actions of a pressurization emergency: masks on, emergency descent, passengers briefed and cared for.
why: A pressurized cabin lets you fly high and comfortably, but a decompression can happen in less than half a second [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]], and then hypoxia is the main danger [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. After a rapid decompression to 25,000 ft you may have only 1.5 to 2.5 minutes to act usefully [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]], and a slow leak can sneak up on you unnoticed [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e]], so the right moves have to be planned and briefed before you need them.

warmup: Think first: you are cruising at 25,000 ft with the cabin at 8,000 ft. A window cracks and the cabin goes to 25,000 ft in a second or two. Your passengers look to you. What do you do in the first five seconds, and why does that order matter more than anything you learned about the system itself?

chunks.title: Why pressurize, and what this Task asks

body.p: Airplanes fly high for two reasons. At high altitude an airplane burns less fuel for a given airspeed, and it can stay in smoother air above bad weather and turbulence. To fly up there, the airplane must be pressurized or carry suitable supplemental oxygen for every occupant [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]].

Pressurization protects the people on board against hypoxia. With the cabin at 8,000 ft or lower, they can ride comfortably for hours with no oxygen equipment. The price is that the crew must always be ready for an accidental loss of cabin pressure [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

body.p: This is a commercial-level Task. The private ACS has no Pressurization Task; it only lists depressurization as one reason for an emergency descent (ACS PA.IX.A.K1).

callout.text: Most commercial checkride airplanes are not pressurized. Then S1 to S3 do not apply, but the knowledge and risk elements still do, so expect an oral scenario: a cabin altitude warning at a high cruising altitude, with passengers on board (ACS CA.VIII.B).

Your commercial certificate does not by itself let you act as PIC of a pressurized airplane whose service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, is above 25,000 ft MSL. That takes logged ground and flight training and two endorsements [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

check.q: Name the two reasons the PHAK gives for flying at high altitude.
check.a: Less fuel burned for a given airspeed, and the chance to fly in smoother air above storms and turbulence [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]].

chunks.title: The parts of the system and their jobs

body.p: In a typical system the cabin, the flight compartment and the baggage compartments form one sealed unit that can hold air at a higher pressure than the air outside [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]].

bullets: Air in: turbine airplanes use bleed air from the engine compressor. Some older turbine airplanes used superchargers. Piston airplanes may use air from the engine turbocharger, sent through a sonic venturi (a flow limiter) [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]].

In most pressurized light airplanes the air comes from the turbocharger's compressor or from an engine-driven pneumatic pump [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]. The AFH notes that some turbocharger models can pressurize the cabin as well as feed the engine [[24:240|AFH 12-9]].

Air out: the outflow valve. By regulating how fast air leaves, it allows a constant inflow of air to the cabin [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]] and keeps the pressure constant by releasing the excess [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]].

Control: cabin altitude is selected manually or, in some airplanes, electronically; a manually set backup control automatically controls the rate of change between cabin and outside pressure [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]].

body.p: Reading the figure (its color code): compressor discharge air from the turbocharger passes the flow control venturi and becomes pressurization air, conditioned air reaches the forward and floor-level outlets, and the outflow valve and the safety/dump valve sit at the back of the cabin, with a line to the cabin altitude controller [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

The cabin pressure control system does five things: it regulates cabin pressure, gives pressure relief and vacuum relief, lets you select the cabin altitude in the isobaric and differential ranges, and dumps cabin pressure. A cabin pressure regulator, an outflow valve and a safety valve do the work [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

head: Safety valve function
What it does
rows: Pressure relief
Keeps cabin pressure from going above a set differential over the outside pressure [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]
Vacuum relief

Lets outside air into the cabin when outside pressure is higher than cabin pressure [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. The AC calls this a negative pressure relief valve, useful after a sudden decompression or in a rapid descent [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]
Dump
Flight deck switch to ram: a solenoid valve opens and dumps cabin air overboard [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]

callout.text: One way in (bleed air or turbocharger air), one controlled way out (outflow valve), and one safety valve that guards both directions and can empty the cabin on purpose [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]] [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

check.q: How does the outflow valve let fresh air keep flowing into a sealed cabin?
check.a: It regulates how fast air leaves, which allows a constant inflow of air to the pressurized area [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

chunks.title: Cabin altitude, differential pressure and the two control ranges

body.p: Keep three altitudes apart. Aircraft altitude is the real height above sea level. Cabin altitude is the cabin's pressure stated as an equivalent altitude. Differential pressure is cabin pressure minus outside pressure [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

A typical system holds a cabin altitude of about 8,000 ft at the airplane's maximum designed cruising altitude. That keeps cabin altitude from changing fast enough to hurt or bother people, and it still lets air move through the cabin quickly enough to clear odors and stale air [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

The chart turns this into arithmetic. Standard pressure is 10.9 psi at 8,000 ft and 4.8 psi at 28,000 ft. Add a 6.1 psi differential to the 4.8 psi outside and the cabin holds 10.9 psi, an 8,000 ft cabin [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

head: Range
What the regulator does
rows: Isobaric range
Holds cabin pressure at the value you selected [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]]
Differential range

Limits cabin pressure to a preset differential. Once the airplane reaches the altitude where the differential equals the fuselage's design maximum, any further climb raises the cabin altitude too [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]] [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]

body.p: Why a limit? The fuselage is built to stand a certain maximum differential. That number comes from the cabin's structural strength and often from how big the cabin is compared with likely rupture areas such as windows and doors [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. Every pressurized airplane has its own maximum differential, and you must know it, along with the manifold pressure settings recommended for different differentials [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]].

callout.text: Cabin pressure = outside pressure + differential. Look up the outside pressure on the chart, add the differential, and look the total back up as an altitude [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

check.q: What sets the maximum differential a fuselage is built to carry?
check.a: The structural strength of the cabin, and often how big the cabin is compared with likely rupture areas such as windows and doors [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

chunks.title: The gauges and the limits you watch

body.p: Three readings work with the controller. The cabin differential pressure gauge shows the difference between inside and outside pressure; watch it so the cabin never goes past the maximum allowable differential. A cabin altimeter checks how well the system is doing. A third instrument shows the cabin rate of climb or descent. Some airplanes combine the differential gauge and the cabin altimeter in one instrument [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

In the figure, the left instrument is a cabin rate-of-climb indicator in thousands of feet per minute. The right one is a combined cabin altitude and differential pressure indicator, with a mark for the maximum cabin differential pressure limit [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

bullets: Cabin altitude is what your body feels and what the oxygen rules count. 14 CFR 91.211 is written in cabin pressure altitudes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

On pressurized airplanes the alternate static source is usually plumbed to a non-pressurized baggage compartment, not the cabin. Using it may cause airspeed, altimeter and VSI errors; the AFM/POH often has a correction table [[24:258|AFH 13-9]].

callout.text: The PHAK says all pressurized aircraft have automatic visual and aural warning systems [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]; the AC says many airplanes have them [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]. Pressurized aircraft that meet certain Part 23 or 25 requirements have a cabin altitude warning that activates at a cabin altitude of 10,000 ft [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]. Check your POH for what yours warns about and when.

check.q: Which gauge tells you the fuselage is near its structural pressure limit?
check.a: The cabin differential pressure gauge. It shows inside minus outside pressure and is watched so the cabin never exceeds the maximum allowable differential [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

chunks.title: Operating the system: a generic flow

body.p: Your POH/AFM gives the real procedure. Plan the pressurization settings for takeoff, climb and descent so you run the system the way the manufacturer recommends [[11:14|AC 61-107B 2-6a]]. The flow below is a generic frame built from the cited facts; anything not cited is application.

bullets: 1. Preflight: look hard at the fuselage, windshield and window panels for cracks or damage that could rupture under pressurization [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12c]]. Test the oxygen system: supply and pressure, regulator, flow, mask fit, and talking to ATC through the mask microphone [[24:309|AFH 15-15]].
2. Brief the passengers on oxygen (chunk 12).
3. Set the controller as the POH says. In the isobaric range the regulator holds the cabin pressure you selected [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].
4. Climb: adjust pressurization with altitude as the POH directs, and scan cabin rate, cabin altitude and differential [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]] [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

5. Cruise: keep monitoring cabin pressurization the whole time above 25,000 ft [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]], and keep the differential below its maximum. If you climb higher at maximum differential, the cabin altitude climbs with you [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]] [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].
6. At each scheduled check (for example hourly or midflight, and before descent), add cabin altitude, differential and oxygen quantity to your 5P review [[1:52|PHAK 2-13]].
7. Descent: plan it early and make it gradual. Keep the cabin rate of descent generally no more than 500 or 600 fpm [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6b]].
8. Before landing: cabin pressure should equal outside pressure, or inner ear injury can result [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6b]].

body.p: Smoke: on pressurized airplanes the pressurization air carries smoke out of the cabin. If the smoke is intense, you may need to depressurize at altitude, if oxygen is available for everyone, or make an emergency descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

callout.text: Say the three numbers out loud on every scan in the climb: cabin altitude, cabin rate, differential. It builds the habit an examiner looks for under S1 (ACS CA.VIII.B.S1).

check.q: Above 25,000 ft MSL, what does AC 61-107B say to emphasize through the whole climb and cruise?

chunks.title: Failure modes and how they show up

body.p: Decompression means the system can no longer hold its designed pressure differential. The cause is either a malfunction in the pressurization system or structural damage to the aircraft [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

head: Problem
What protects or warns you
rows: Cabin pressure trying to go above the set differential
Pressure relief in the safety valve [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]
Outside pressure higher than cabin pressure
Vacuum relief lets outside air in [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]
Structural damage at a window or door
The maximum differential is set partly by likely rupture areas such as windows and doors [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]; people near an opening can be tossed or blown out [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Any loss of pressure
Automatic visual and aural warnings. The PHAK says all pressurized aircraft have them [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]; the AC says many airplanes do [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]

body.p: Turbocharger failure: higher oil temperature, lower oil pressure and a drop in manifold pressure can point to it. You may not be able to hold altitude, and if the pressurization depends on the turbocharger compressor, you can lose cabin pressure too. Watch the cabin closely during the descent so a slow decompression does not make you hypoxic, and tell ATC you are descending [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]].

head: Decompression type
How it shows up
rows: Explosive
Faster than the lungs; more likely in small cabins [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]]
Rapid
Slower than the lungs; much lower risk of lung damage [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]]
Gradual or slow
May not be detected; warning systems generally give the indication [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]]

body.p: Whatever the cause, the main danger of decompression is hypoxia. Quick, proper use of oxygen equipment prevents unconsciousness, and a rapid descent keeps the other problems small [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

callout.text: The AC warns that a slow decompression is as dangerous as, or more dangerous than, a rapid or explosive one. The usual noise and fog may be missing, and hypoxia dulls your ability to recognize the emergency [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]] [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]. The cabin altimeter and the warning system may be your only clues [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]] [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

check.q: In a slow decompression with no noise and no fog, what does the AC say generally gives you the indication?
check.a: Automatic visual and aural warning systems [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

body.p: Physiologically, decompressions come in two kinds, set by how fast the cabin empties compared with your lungs. With no restriction such as a mask, the lungs normally need about 0.2 seconds to release air [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

head: Type
Definition
Notes
rows: Explosive
Cabin pressure changes faster than the lungs can decompress [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]
Possible lung damage. Most authorities treat any decompression under 0.5 seconds as explosive and potentially dangerous [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]
Rapid
The lungs decompress faster than the cabin [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]
Oxygen in the lungs is exhaled fast, so the time you can act usefully gets shorter [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]

body.p: What people notice in an explosive decompression: maybe noise and a moment of feeling dazed. The cabin fills with fog, dust or flying debris. The fog comes from the sudden drop in temperature and the change in relative humidity. Ears normally clear by themselves, and air rushes out of the mouth and nose as the lungs empty [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

If structure fails, people near an opening can be tossed or blown out, so the PHAK says people near openings should wear a seat belt or harness at all times while seated in a pressurized airplane. Wind blast and extreme cold come with the hole [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Anything loose moves toward the opening and can hurt people, so secure baggage and oxygen cylinders [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]] [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

head: Factor (all else equal)
Effect on how fast the cabin decompresses
rows: Bigger opening
Smaller cabin
Greater pressure differential
Slower, per the AC [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]
Compressors still pumping air in
The inflow rate sets how fast pressure is lost [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]
Higher altitude
Faster, with less resistance to air leaving [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]

body.p: Cabin size matters a lot for the airplanes you will fly. With the same hole, a typical small pressurized airplane can decompress about 10 to 200 times faster than a large one, so its crew will probably have less time for lifesaving actions [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

Gas expansion: as pressure drops, gas in the body expands, most noticeably in the ears and the gut [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]. If it cannot escape, pressure builds and hurts: ear pain, sinus pain and a short-term loss of hearing [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

callout.text: Fog after a sudden pressure loss comes from the temperature drop and the change in humidity [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]; do not mistake it for smoke (application). Masks first; sort out the rest after you have oxygen.

check.q: Why does the AC say to secure baggage and oxygen cylinders in a pressurized airplane?
check.a: In an explosive decompression with a large opening, anything loose moves toward the opening as flying debris and can injure people [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]] [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

chunks.title: Hypoxia after a pressure loss: impairment and symptoms

body.p: Altitude hypoxia comes only from low barometric pressure. The air is still about 21 percent oxygen all the way up [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. So when the cabin goes to flight altitude, the cabin altitude, not the airplane's, decides how impaired you get.

head: Cabin altitude
Typical effect on a healthy pilot (AIM)
rows: From 5,000 ft
Night vision gets worse [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]
Below 12,000 ft
Other significant effects usually do not appear [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]

Judgment, memory, alertness, coordination and calculation suffer; headache, drowsiness, dizziness, euphoria or belligerence. Performance can seriously drop within 15 minutes at 15,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]
Above 15,000 ft
Tunnel vision and blue fingernails and lips (cyanosis) [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]

body.p: The PHAK lists common symptoms: cyanosis, headache, slower reactions, impaired judgment, euphoria, visual impairment, drowsiness, dizziness, and tingling or numbness. The first ones can be euphoria and a carefree feeling. As it gets worse, vision narrows, instruments get hard to read, and you may still believe everything is normal [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Some things make it worse: carbon monoxide, anemia, some medicines, small amounts of alcohol, and depressant drugs. Heat, cold, fever and anxiety raise your oxygen demand [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]].
The AIM says a person's own hypoxia symptoms stay the same from one exposure to the next, so seeing them in an altitude chamber helps you recognize them later [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

Treatment: if you suspect hypoxia, put on the mask right away, breathe 100 percent oxygen slowly, and descend to a safe altitude. Recovery usually takes only seconds once you are on 100 percent oxygen. With no oxygen available, make an emergency descent to below 10,000 ft MSL, and land as soon as possible if symptoms persist [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. After a severe exposure, symptoms can seem to get worse for 15 to 60 seconds after you start 100 percent oxygen; keep breathing it slowly anyway [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]].

callout.text: Feeling great at altitude after a warning is a symptom, not a reassurance [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

check.q: After a pressure loss you feel carefree and sure all is well. What could that be?
check.a: Early hypoxia. Euphoria and a carefree feeling can be the first symptoms, and hypoxia can give a false sense that everything is normal [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

chunks.title: Time of useful consciousness as a planning number

body.p: Time of useful consciousness is the most time you have to make and carry out rational, life-saving decisions at an altitude without supplemental oxygen. Above 10,000 ft the symptoms get worse and that time drops fast [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. The AC also calls it effective performance time: from the moment the oxygen supply stops until you can no longer take proper corrective and protective action [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e]].

bullets: Read the right column. As a general rule, TUC after a decompression to between 25,000 and 43,000 ft is cut by 50 percent; above 43,000 ft it is about 9 to 12 seconds [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7e]].
The values are averages with wide differences between people, so assume the lower number is the one that limits you [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].
TUC is not the moment you pass out. Impairment can start right away, so use 100 percent oxygen promptly [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e]].

TUC gets shorter with a faster ascent, a faster decompression, physical activity, fatigue, low blood sugar, alcohol, some medicines, smoking, poor fitness and illness. Ten deep knee bends at 25,000 ft without a mask can halve it [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7e]].

body.p: At the low end, the AIM says the ability to take corrective action is lost in 20 to 30 minutes at 18,000 ft and 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]], while the PHAK table lists 30 minutes or more at 20,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Plan with the shorter numbers.

head: Planning question
Why TUC answers it
rows: Where are the masks?
At 25,000 ft the AC gives 1.5 to 2.5 minutes after a rapid decompression [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. A mask stowed out of reach can cost all of it.
Are they tested?
A preflight functional test checks supply, pressure, regulator, flow, mask fit and the mask microphone [[24:309|AFH 15-15]].
Who helps the passengers?
No one, if they were not briefed; you will be busy flying and on oxygen (application).
How long to a safe altitude?
Know your descent rate and how long it takes (see the calc game); TUC is not time to troubleshoot (application).
What is below the route?
High terrain may keep you above 12,500, 14,000 or 15,000 ft cabin altitude for longer, and those are the oxygen thresholds [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

callout.text: Above FL 250 in a pressurized cabin, at least a 10-minute supply of oxygen must be available for each occupant for a descent after losing pressurization, in addition to the oxygen required by 91.211(a) [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

check.q: Using AC Figure 2-3, how much time of useful consciousness do you have at 35,000 ft after a rapid decompression, and which value do you plan with?
check.a: 15 to 30 seconds, and you plan with the lower value, 15 seconds [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

body.p: Besides hypoxia, a high-altitude decompression brings evolved gas decompression sickness: when pressure on the body drops far enough, nitrogen comes out of solution and forms bubbles that can harm body tissues [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. It can follow a rapid decompression or flying an unpressurized airplane to altitude. The most common symptom is joint pain, called the bends [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

bullets: Put on the oxygen mask right away and set the regulator to 100 percent [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
Start an emergency descent and land as soon as possible. Even if the symptoms go away during the descent, land and get a medical evaluation while still breathing oxygen [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
With joint pain, keep the joint still; do not try to work the pain out [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
After landing, see an FAA medical officer, an AME, a military flight surgeon or a hyperbaric medicine specialist; treatment may need a hyperbaric chamber [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
Symptoms can show up later, after you are back on the ground [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

body.p: Pressurized airplanes are not immune. A sudden loss of cabin pressure can cause altitude DCS, and a rapid decompression above 18,000 ft carries more risk than reaching the same altitude slowly [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:33|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. After an in-flight rapid decompression, do not fly for at least 24 hours, and watch for delayed signs; get medical help right away if they appear [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

callout.text: Neurologic DCS, the chokes and mottled or marbled skin are very serious and can be fatal if untreated [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

body.p: This is also why the AIM's waiting times after scuba diving use actual flight altitude, not cabin altitude: they allow for the chance that the airplane decompresses [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

check.q: After landing with a suspected DCS case, which kinds of doctors does the PHAK say to seek out?
check.a: An FAA medical officer, an AME, a military flight surgeon or a hyperbaric medicine specialist; a doctor not trained in aviation or hypobaric medicine may not know the problem [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

body.p: The main danger is hypoxia, so oxygen comes first, then a rapid descent [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. The AC's common emergency procedure fits on one line: don the mask in 5 seconds or less, check for flow and breathe 100 percent oxygen; descend, preferably below 10,000 ft; land as soon as possible where medical help is available [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]. Recovery is similar for every type of decompression, and it starts with recognizing it: the event, the cabin altitude warning, or your own hypoxia symptoms [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]].

An emergency descent gets you down as fast as possible without exceeding structural limits; a sudden loss of cabin pressure is one reason to fly it. Use the manufacturer's procedure. In general: roll into about 30 to 45 degrees of bank to keep positive load factors, power to idle unless the manufacturer says otherwise, propeller (if equipped) to low pitch, high rpm so it acts as a brake, and gear and flaps as recommended [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

bullets: Do not exceed VNE, VLE or VFE as they apply; in turbulence, also respect VA [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
Start the recovery high enough to level off safely or to set up a precautionary landing [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

Reaching a safe altitude comes first, but know that a rapid descent from high altitude can cold-shock a piston engine and crack cylinders [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]]. In training, stop once the descent is established; prolonged practice overcools the cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].
Checkride link: the emergency descent Task asks for 30 to 45 degrees of bank, airspeed +0/-10 knots, and a level-off within 100 feet (ACS CA.IX.A.S4, S5).

body.p: Talk once the airplane is under control: MAYDAY, said three times, is the distress signal; give the nature of the problem, your intentions and the help you want [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. In an in-flight emergency needing immediate action, you may deviate from any Part 91 rule as far as the emergency requires, and send a written report if the FAA asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

callout.text: Flight training for 61.31(g) includes emergency procedures for a simulated rapid decompression, done without actually depressurizing the airplane, and emergency descent procedures [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. The AC says never depressurize for training: simulate it by donning masks, turning on the oxygen, configuring and flying the descent, coordinate with ATC first, and do not leave an assigned altitude without a clearance [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

check.q: How high should you start the recovery from an emergency descent?
check.a: High enough to make sure of a safe return to level flight or a precautionary landing [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

body.p: In a decompression you may have only minutes, or less, to act usefully [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]], and you will be flying. Passengers have to know what to do without you (application).

Rules that name it: Part 135 requires a briefing on the normal and emergency use of oxygen when the flight goes above 12,000 ft MSL [[6:36|14 CFR 135.117]]. Part 91 requires it in large airplanes and turbojet multiengine airplanes [[60:534|14 CFR 91.519]] [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501]]. For a small Part 91 single, the sources here name no such rule, but the ACS asks you to give it (ACS CA.VIII.B.S3).

bullets: Where the masks are, how to put one on and how to tell oxygen is flowing (the preflight check covers mask fit and flow) [[24:309|AFH 15-15]].
When to put it on: at the warning, at your call, or at a bang, fog or rush of air [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].
Mask on first, then help a neighbor: hypoxia can feel fine while it disables you [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] (application).
Seat belt fastened at all times while seated, especially anyone near a window or door [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].
No smoking anywhere near oxygen; oils and greases can ignite in oxygen [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].
Ears may hurt with pressure changes; swallow, yawn, or pinch the nose and blow gently (Valsalva) [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].
Tell the pilot about joint pain, tingling, chest pain or itching after any pressure loss [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]].

callout.text: Sample close to your briefing: 'If you hear the horn, see fog or I say masks, put yours on first, then help your neighbor. Keep your belt on while seated. Tell me about any pain or tingling.'

check.q: Which Part 91 airplanes must have an oral passenger briefing that covers the oxygen equipment?
check.a: Large airplanes and turbojet-powered multiengine airplanes under subpart F; the briefing covers the normal and emergency use of the installed oxygen equipment [[60:534|14 CFR 91.519]] [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501]].

chunks.title: The rules that tie in: 91.211(b) and 61.31(g)

head: Rule
What it requires
rows: Above FL 250: at least a 10-minute oxygen supply for each occupant for a descent after losing pressurization, on top of what 91.211(a) requires [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]

Above FL 350: one pilot at the controls wears and uses a sealed mask that supplies oxygen all the time or automatically when the cabin goes above 14,000 ft. Exception up to FL 410: two pilots at the controls, each with a quick-donning mask that goes on with one hand within 5 seconds [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211(b)]]
Above FL 350, if one pilot leaves the controls, the other puts on and uses a mask until that pilot returns [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211(b)]]

Logged ground training and an endorsement: high-altitude aerodynamics and weather, respiration, hypoxia, duration of consciousness without oxygen, prolonged oxygen use, gas expansion and bubbles, prevention, and decompression [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]

Logged flight training and an endorsement, in a pressurized airplane or a representative simulator or FTD: cruise above 25,000 ft, simulated rapid decompression, emergency descent [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]

Not needed if you can document PIC time or a proficiency check in a pressurized aircraft before April 15, 1991, a military PIC check, or a Part 121, 125 or 135 PIC proficiency check [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31(g)(3)]]

body.p: The trigger for 61.31(g) is a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 ft MSL [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. Both numbers are in the AFM, and a maximum operating altitude is limited to 25,000 ft or lower unless certain airworthiness standards are met [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]]. The AC recommends the same training for every pilot who flies above 10,000 ft MSL [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]].

91.211(a) counts cabin pressure altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. After a pressure loss, the oxygen rules follow the cabin's new altitude, not the altitude you planned. The details of those rules belong to the Supplemental Oxygen Task (CA.VIII.A).

callout.text: Commercial context: in a Part 135 pressurized aircraft, once cabin pressure altitude goes above 10,000 ft each pilot must follow the unpressurized oxygen rules of 135.89(a) [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]].

check.q: An airplane's maximum operating altitude is 25,000 ft and its service ceiling is 27,000 ft. Does 61.31(g) apply?
check.a: No. The lower of the two is 25,000 ft, and the rule applies only when that lower number is above 25,000 ft MSL [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

body.p: SRM is managing every resource you have, on board and outside, before and during flight. For a single pilot, the autopilot and ATC play the part of the other crew member [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]]. Never let anyone else, not ATC and not your passengers, make risk decisions for you [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].

Plan the decision points: the 5P check is done preflight, before takeoff, hourly or at midflight, before descent, and before the final approach fix or pattern entry [[1:52|PHAK 2-13]]. At high altitude, add cabin altitude, differential and oxygen to each one (application).

head: Common error
Fix
rows: Troubleshooting the controller before putting on the mask
Mask on in 5 seconds or less; hypoxia is the main danger [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]] [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Diving the cabin down fast in a normal descent
Plan a gradual descent, cabin rate generally 500 to 600 fpm or less, and equalize before landing [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6b]]
Scanning only the airplane altimeter
Scan cabin altitude, cabin rate and differential too [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]
Taking a quiet cabin as proof all is fine
Trust the warning and the gauges; hypoxia feels normal [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]
Speed past VLE, VFE or VA in the descent
Fly the POH configuration and respect each limit [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Skipping the passenger oxygen briefing
Brief every flight that could need oxygen (ACS CA.VIII.B.S3)
Continuing after DCS symptoms fade
Land and get evaluated while on oxygen [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
Leveling off late
Start the recovery early enough to level within 100 ft (ACS CA.IX.A.S5) [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]

callout.text: In a two-pilot cockpit, the AC highly recommends standard callouts in every phase of flight [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]. Agree before takeoff who flies and who handles ATC and the checklist if the warning goes off. That is the CRM half of S4 (ACS CA.VIII.B.S4).

scenario.title: The mountain charter in a pressurized turboprop single
scenario.setup: You just got your commercial certificate and an operator offers you a Part 91 trip flying a pressurized single-engine turboprop. Its AFM lists a maximum operating altitude of FL 300. You have never flown a pressurized airplane. The owner wants FL 280 for the winds, with four passengers, on a route that crosses high mountains for about 80 nm. One passenger mentions a bad head cold.

questions.q: Can you act as PIC on this trip with your new commercial certificate?
questions.a: Not yet. The lower of service ceiling and maximum operating altitude is above 25,000 ft, so you need logged ground training and flight training (cruise above 25,000 ft, simulated rapid decompression, emergency descent), each with an endorsement [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]], unless a 61.31(g)(3) exception fits you [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31(g)(3)]].

questions.q: On preflight, what do you look at hardest on this pressurized airplane?
questions.a: The fuselage, windshield and window panels for any crack or damage that could rupture under pressurization, and the oxygen equipment: available supply, an operational check, masks within reach, and talking to ATC through the mask microphone [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12c]] [[24:309|AFH 15-15]].

questions.q: Why do the mountains change your oxygen planning?
questions.a: After a pressure loss you may not be able to descend below 12,500, 14,000 or 15,000 ft cabin altitude until past the high terrain, and 91.211(a) applies by cabin pressure altitude: crew oxygen after 30 minutes above 12,500 ft, crew oxygen the whole time above 14,000 ft, and oxygen provided for every occupant above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. Plan enough oxygen, or a route and altitude that allow a quick descent (application).

questions.q: How much time of useful consciousness do you plan on at FL 280 if the cabin depressurizes?
questions.a: After a rapid decompression at 28,000 ft the AC gives 1 to 1.5 minutes, and you plan with the lower value [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. So masks go on in 5 seconds or less, before any troubleshooting [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]].

questions.q: In the briefing, a passenger in the window seat asks why he has to keep his belt on in smooth air. What do you tell him?
questions.a: If a window or door fails, people near the opening can be tossed or blown out, so the PHAK says people near openings should wear a belt or harness at all times while seated in a pressurized airplane [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Loose items also fly toward the opening, so stow his bag [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]].

questions.q: What about the passenger with the cold?
questions.a: Congestion can cause an ear block, with severe pain and hearing loss, and the AIM says the prevention is not flying with an upper respiratory infection; decongestant sprays usually do not protect enough [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. A fast emergency descent would make it worse, so advise the passenger not to fly (application).

skills.do: If the airplane has a pressurization system, operate it as the POH says: set the controller, then keep scanning cabin altitude, cabin rate and differential, and keep the differential below its limit.
skills.practice: On every high-altitude flight, call out cabin altitude, cabin rate and differential at each climb and cruise scan, and plan descents that keep the cabin rate at or below 500 to 600 fpm with the cabin equalized before landing [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]] [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6b]].

skills.do: If installed, respond to a simulated pressurization failure the right way: mask on and 100 percent oxygen first, then a POH emergency descent within its limits, then ATC.
skills.practice: Rehearse the flow out loud with a CFI until the mask is on in 5 seconds or less [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]; fly emergency descents to the ACS standard of 30 to 45 degrees of bank, +0/-10 knots and a level-off within 100 ft (ACS CA.IX.A.S4, S5) [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

skills.do: If installed, brief passengers on using supplemental oxygen if pressurization fails.
skills.practice: Write a 30-second oxygen briefing for your airplane and give it to friends before every high flight; check they can find and put on a mask [[24:309|AFH 15-15]] [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

skills.do: Use SRM or CRM: use the autopilot, ATC and any crew member, divide tasks, and keep risk decisions in your own hands.
skills.practice: Brief before takeoff who does what if the cabin warning sounds, and include cabin and oxygen checks in each 5P review [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]] [[1:52|PHAK 2-13]].

quiz.q: In a typical pressurized piston airplane, where does the cabin air come from?
options: Bleed air from the engine compressor
Ram air through the dump valve
The engine turbocharger, through a sonic venturi
A separate electric cabin compressor
quiz.why: Piston airplanes may use air from the turbocharger sent through a sonic venturi (flow limiter); bleed air is the turbine method [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]].

quiz.q: What does the cabin pressure regulator do in the isobaric range?
options: Holds the maximum differential pressure
Holds cabin pressure at the value you selected
Dumps cabin pressure overboard
Lets outside air in when it is at a higher pressure
quiz.why: In the isobaric range the regulator controls cabin pressure to a selected value; in the differential range it limits it to a preset differential [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

quiz.q: You move the flight deck dump switch to ram. What happens?
options: The outflow valve closes fully
The vacuum relief valve opens to let outside air in
A solenoid valve opens and cabin air is dumped overboard
The turbocharger stops sending air to the cabin
quiz.why: With the switch at ram, a solenoid valve opens and the dump valve releases cabin air into the atmosphere [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

quiz.q: According to AC 61-107B, what should the cabin pressure be before you land?
options: Equal to the outside pressure
Held at 8,000 ft cabin altitude
At the maximum differential
1 psi above the outside pressure
quiz.why: Before landing, cabin pressure should equal ambient pressure or inner ear injury can result; plan gradual descents with the cabin rate generally no more than 500 or 600 fpm [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6b]].

quiz.q: Which instrument does the PHAK describe as a check on how well the pressurization system is performing?
options: The oxygen cylinder pressure gauge
The turbine inlet temperature gauge
The airplane's main altimeter
The cabin altimeter
quiz.why: A cabin altimeter is provided as a check on the performance of the system, alongside the differential gauge and the cabin rate instrument [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

quiz.q: Per AC 61-107B, with all other factors equal, which makes a cabin decompress faster?
options: A larger cabin
A smaller opening
A higher altitude
A lower altitude
quiz.why: Higher altitude gives a faster decompression because there is less resistance to the air leaving. A larger cabin and a smaller opening both slow it [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]].

quiz.q: Per AC 61-107B Figure 2-3, how much time of useful consciousness do you have at 22,000 ft following a rapid decompression?
options: 10 minutes
5 to 6 minutes
1.5 to 2.5 minutes
20 to 30 minutes
quiz.why: At 22,000 ft the table gives 10 minutes, but 5 to 6 minutes following a rapid decompression [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

quiz.q: What is the most common symptom of altitude decompression sickness?
options: Itching skin
Blue fingernails
Dry cough
Joint pain (the bends)
quiz.why: The most common symptom is joint pain, known as the bends [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

quiz.q: Per AC 61-107B, how does a rapid decompression above 18,000 ft change the risk of altitude decompression sickness?
options: It is smaller, because the exposure is short
It is greater than reaching the same altitude slowly
It is the same as reaching the altitude slowly
There is none in a pressurized airplane
quiz.why: A rapid decompression (a high rate of ascent) above 18,000 ft carries a greater DCS risk than the same altitude reached more slowly [[11:33|AC 61-107B 2-7]], and DCS can follow a loss of pressure even in a pressurized airplane [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

quiz.q: For 61.31(g) flight training, how is the rapid decompression practiced?
options: By opening the dump valve at FL 250 and practicing the emergency descent with masks on
As a simulated rapid decompression, without depressurizing the airplane
Only in an altitude chamber, never in the airplane, with an instructor observing
By shutting off the turbocharger air at cruise to cause a slow loss of cabin pressure
quiz.why: The flight training covers proper emergency procedures for a simulated rapid decompression without actually depressurizing the aircraft, plus emergency descent [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

final_quiz.q: A pressurized airplane's maximum differential is 6.0 psi. Using the standard pressure chart, which is the highest of these altitudes that still keeps the cabin at or below 8,000 ft?
final_quiz.why: An 8,000 ft cabin needs 10.9 psi. At 26,000 ft: 5.2 + 6.0 = 11.2 psi, more than 10.9, so the cabin is below 8,000 ft. At 28,000 ft: 4.8 + 6.0 = 10.8 psi, less than 10.9, so the cabin is above 8,000 ft [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

final_quiz.q: Two pilots fly a pressurized jet at FL 370, each with a quick-donning mask. The captain leaves the flight deck for a few minutes. What does 91.211(b) require?
options: The pilot at the controls wears and uses a mask until the captain returns
Nothing, because quick-donning masks within reach satisfy the rule for both pilots
Both pilots must wear masks for the rest of the flight once one has left the controls
A descent to FL 350 or below before the captain is allowed to leave the flight deck
final_quiz.why: Above FL 350, if one pilot leaves the controls for any reason, the remaining pilot at the controls must put on and use an oxygen mask until the other returns [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211(b)]].

final_quiz.q: You hear the cabin altitude warning at FL 240. There was no bang and no fog, and you feel fine. What is the best first action?
options: Ask a passenger whether anything changed in the cabin before you act on the alarm
Look up the controller troubleshooting checklist first, then decide whether to use oxygen
Put on your oxygen mask, then check the cabin altitude and differential
Silence the warning and keep watching for symptoms before taking any other action
final_quiz.why: A slow decompression may lack the noise and fog and is as dangerous as, or more dangerous than, a rapid one, because hypoxia dulls recognition [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]] [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]; warning systems generally give the indication [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]]. If hypoxia is suspected, don the mask and breathe 100 percent oxygen first [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

final_quiz.q: You open the alternate static source in a pressurized airplane. What should you know?
options: It vents to the pressurized cabin, so the instruments read the cabin altitude and airspeed errors are not a concern
It dumps cabin pressure overboard through the static line, so use it only to depressurize
Usually plumbed to a non-pressurized baggage compartment; errors may appear, so check the AFM/POH table
It can only be used on the ground, because airborne it connects to the cabin differential gauge
final_quiz.why: On pressurized airplanes the alternate static source is usually plumbed to a non-pressurized baggage compartment. Using it may create airspeed, altimeter or VSI errors, and a correction table is often in the AFM/POH [[24:258|AFH 13-9]].

final_quiz.q: After a decompression and descent, a passenger reports tingling that started in her feet and is moving up her legs. The symptoms ease as you level at 10,000 ft. What do you do?
options: Continue; the descent fixed it, and tingling that eases is harmless
Climb back to cruise altitude once she feels better, since the symptoms have clearly stopped
Have her walk around the cabin to work out the tingling and restore circulation
Keep her on 100 percent oxygen, land as soon as possible, and get medical evaluation
final_quiz.why: Rising tingling from the feet is a spinal cord (neurologic) DCS sign [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]]. Even if symptoms go away, land and seek medical evaluation while continuing oxygen [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

final_quiz.q: At FL 230 in a pressurized piston single, oil temperature rises, oil pressure drops and manifold pressure falls. Your cabin air comes from the turbocharger compressor. What else must you watch as you descend?
options: Cabin pressure: it can be lost, causing hypoxia from a slow decompression
Only the vacuum relief function, since cabin pressure itself cannot be affected by the engine
Only the propeller rpm, since the oil and manifold signs affect nothing else aboard
Nothing; pressurization is independent of the turbocharger, so no cabin check is needed
final_quiz.why: Those signs can mean a turbocharger failure. If the pressurization depends on the turbocharger compressor, cabin pressure can be lost, so monitor it during the descent to avoid hypoxia from a slow decompression, and tell ATC you are descending [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]].

final_quiz.q: You will fly a single-engine jet alone at FL 360. What does 91.211(b) require?
options: Nothing beyond the 10-minute supply for each occupant, because the pressurized cabin keeps you below 10,000 ft
Only a quick-donning mask within reach of your seat, which is enough for a single pilot up to FL 410
A sealed mask worn and used at the controls, supplying oxygen always or automatically above 14,000 ft cabin
A mask only if the cabin altitude exceeds 10,000 ft, and then only for the part of the flight above it
final_quiz.why: Above FL 350 one pilot at the controls wears and uses a secured, sealed mask that supplies oxygen at all times or automatically above 14,000 ft cabin; the quick-donning exception needs two pilots at the controls and applies only up to FL 410 [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211(b)]].

final_quiz.q: After a severe hypoxia exposure you get your mask on at 100 percent. For about 30 seconds you feel worse. What does AC 61-107B say?
options: The oxygen is contaminated; take the mask off at once and switch to the passenger oxygen system
The apparent worsening can last 15 to 60 seconds; keep breathing 100 percent oxygen
It means you are hyperventilating, so switch the regulator to normal and breathe faster
It proves you have decompression sickness, not hypoxia, so stop the oxygen and descend
final_quiz.why: After an extreme hypoxia exposure, 100 percent oxygen can cause an apparent increase in symptoms for 15 to 60 seconds. The recovery stays the same: breathe 100 percent oxygen and breathe slowly [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]].

final_quiz.q: Compared with an airliner, how fast can a typical small pressurized airplane decompress through the same size hole, per AC 61-107B?
options: On the order of 10 to 200 times faster
About twice as fast
About the same
Slower, because its cabin is small
final_quiz.why: Under the same conditions a typical small pressurized aircraft can decompress on the order of 10 to 200 times faster than large aircraft, so its crew will probably have less time for lifesaving actions [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

final_quiz.q: Your last PIC proficiency check under Part 135 was in a pressurized airplane. You now want to fly a Part 91 pressurized single with a service ceiling of FL 300. What about 61.31(g)?
options: The training and endorsements are not required, since you can document that check
You need only the ground training endorsement, because the flight portion is waived
You still need both the ground and flight training endorsements before you act as PIC
61.31(g) applies only to Part 135 flights, so it does not reach your Part 91 flight
final_quiz.why: The 61.31(g)(1) and (2) training is not required for a person who can document a PIC proficiency check under Part 121, 125 or 135 in a pressurized aircraft [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31(g)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane had a real rapid decompression at FL 250 yesterday afternoon. You landed safely and everyone feels fine. The owner wants you to fly the same passengers out at 0800 today, about 16 hours later. What does AC 61-107B advise?
options: Fine, as long as you stay below 8,000 ft cabin altitude for the entire flight
Do not fly for at least 24 hours, and watch for delayed DCS signs
Fine, since no one had symptoms in flight and everyone feels well this morning
Fly, but keep everyone on oxygen and stay below 10,000 ft for the whole trip
final_quiz.why: After an in-flight rapid decompression, do not fly for at least 24 hours, and stay alert for delayed signs of altitude DCS [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Delayed symptoms can appear after return to ground level [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

final_quiz.q: Single pilot at FL 250, the cabin decompresses. Which choice best shows SRM?
options: After your mask is on, use the autopilot and ATC to help manage the descent
Let a passenger choose the diversion airport and read the checklist while you fly
Put off any ATC call until you are on the ground and the situation is stable
Refuse ATC help, to keep the frequency clear and avoid distracting yourself
final_quiz.why: SRM means using all resources; for a single pilot, the autopilot and ATC replicate CRM, and you never hand risk decisions to passengers or ATC [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]]. Oxygen comes first [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

final_quiz.q: Right after a rapid decompression, a passenger says his stomach feels bloated and his ears feel full. What does AC 61-107B say explains this?
options: The chokes, a type of decompression sickness that shows up as bloating and ear fullness
Hyperventilation from the stress of the event, which causes the stomach and ear symptoms
Carbon monoxide from the heater, which acts on the stomach and inner ear
Gas expanding as pressure drops, most noticeable in the ears and GI tract
final_quiz.why: Gas expands as pressure decreases, and it is most noticeable in the ears and the GI tract [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]. The chokes are a lung problem: deep chest pain, pain on breathing and coughing [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]].

takeaways: Pressurization adds a differential to outside pressure; cabin pressure = outside + differential, read on the standard pressure chart.
Isobaric range holds your selected cabin; at maximum differential, any climb raises the cabin altitude.
Outflow valve lets air out at a set rate; the safety valve gives pressure relief, vacuum relief and dump.
Decompression: explosive is faster than the lungs, rapid is slower, and slow may not be noticed at all; hypoxia is the main danger every time.
Time of useful consciousness is minutes or seconds up high and about half that after a rapid decompression: mask on in 5 seconds.
Then an emergency descent within VNE, VLE, VFE and VA, a MAYDAY call, and medical care for any DCS signs.
Brief passengers on oxygen, and meet 91.211(b) and 61.31(g) before you fly high.
cfi_notes: Most checkrides are flown in unpressurized airplanes, so S1 to S3 and R2 drop out ('if equipment is installed'), but the K elements and R1 stay. Run this Task as an oral scenario tied to the emergency descent Task (CA.IX.A). Drill the masks-on reflex on the ground with the real masks, timed; it is the single most valuable habit in this Task.

The PHAK says a rapid decompression reduces effective performance time 'by one-third to one-fourth its normal time' [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]], which can be read as 'to' or 'by'. AC 61-107B is clearer: TUC after a decompression to 25,000 to 43,000 ft is reduced by 50 percent, by at least 50 percent per its list of factors [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]] [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]. Teach the AC numbers and its Figure 2-3.

The PHAK lists only explosive and rapid decompression [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]; AC 61-107B adds the gradual or slow kind and warns that a slow decompression is as dangerous as or more dangerous than a rapid one [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]. Make sure students do not think 'no bang, no emergency'.

AC 61-107B 2-7e lists 'pressure differential' as a decompression rate factor and says only that, with all other factors equal, greater pressure differential means slower decompression [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]. It gives no reason. Teach the sentence as written, do not add an explanation, and do not quiz it.

The PHAK glossary calls rapid decompression 'the almost instantaneous loss of cabin pressure' [[1:501|PHAK G-25]], while chapter 7 separates explosive from rapid by comparing the cabin with the lungs [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. Teach the chapter 7 definitions, which match the ACS's focus on effects on crew and passengers.

The PHAK says automatic visual and aural warning systems are in all pressurized aircraft [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]], but AC 61-107B says many airplanes have them, and that the 10,000 ft cabin altitude warning comes with certain Part 23 or 25 requirements [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]. Teach the AC: check the POH for what your airplane has.

The PHAK TUC table lists 30 minutes or more at 20,000 ft and 5 to 10 minutes at 22,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]; the AIM says corrective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]], and AC 61-107B Figure 2-3 gives 10 minutes at 22,000 ft [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. Plan with the AIM and the AC figure, and with the lower value.
Students mix up airplane altitude and cabin altitude. Have them say which altimeter they mean, and point out that 91.211(a) is written in cabin pressure altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

The AFH-3C has no separate high-altitude chapter; its high-altitude material is a short training outline in the turboprop chapter [[24:308|AFH 15-14]]. AC 61-107B, which the ACS lists as a reference, is the deeper source; its chapter 2 is written for single-engine and light twin airplanes [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]].
gaps: Controller settings, cabin altitude selection for landing, warning thresholds, maximum differential and emergency descent speeds and configuration are airplane-specific; use the POH/AFM.
How fast a given airplane will decompress is not something you can look up; AC 61-107B says actual decompression times are hard to calculate because of the many variables [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].
No source here gives a standard passenger oxygen briefing script for small Part 91 airplanes; the ACS asks for one, so build it from the POH and the cited facts.
The 10,000 ft cabin altitude warning applies to aircraft meeting certain Part 23 or 25 requirements [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]; older or other airplanes may warn differently, so check the POH.
The sources do not say whether an autopilot should fly the emergency descent; that depends on the airplane and its AFM.

activities.title: Work the pressurization numbers
activities.intro: Use the standard pressure chart (Figure 7-41). Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your airplane's maximum differential is 5.0 psi. At 20,000 ft at maximum differential, what is the cabin altitude? (No interpolation needed.)
items.why: Outside at 20,000 ft = 6.8 psi. 6.8 + 5.0 = 11.8 psi, which the chart lists at 6,000 ft [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

items.q: Your airplane's maximum differential is 5.5 psi. You cruise at 26,000 ft at maximum differential. What is the cabin altitude? Interpolate linearly between the 8,000 and 10,000 ft rows of the chart.
Same airplane (maximum differential 5.5 psi), now climbing to 30,000 ft at maximum differential. What is the cabin altitude? Interpolate linearly between the 10,000 and 12,000 ft rows.
items.why: Outside 4.4 + 5.5 = 9.9 psi. Between 10,000 ft (10.1) and 12,000 ft (9.4): (10.1 - 9.9) / (10.1 - 9.4) = 0.2 / 0.7 = 0.286, and 10,000 + 0.286 x 2,000 = 10,571 ft. At maximum differential, climbing raises the cabin altitude [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]] [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

items.q: AC 61-107B Table 2-8 lists a B-747 cabin of 59,000 cubic ft and a Learjet cabin of 265 cubic ft. How many times bigger is the B-747 cabin? (Round to a whole number.)
items.why: 59,000 / 265 = 222.6, about 223, the 223:1 ratio in the table. With the same hole, the small cabin empties much faster, so its crew has less time to act [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

items.q: TUC at 30,000 ft is 1 to 2 minutes. Using the AC rule that a decompression between 25,000 and 43,000 ft cuts TUC by 50 percent, and planning with the lower value, how many seconds do you have?
items.why: Lower value 1 minute = 60 s. 60 x 0.5 = 30 s, which matches the 30 s to 1 min shown following rapid decompression [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

items.q: Cruise cabin altitude is 8,000 ft and the destination field is at 1,000 ft. Holding the cabin descent rate to 500 fpm, how many minutes does the cabin need to reach field elevation so it is equalized before landing?
items.why: 8,000 - 1,000 = 7,000 ft. 7,000 / 500 = 14 minutes. Cabin descent rates should generally not exceed 500 or 600 fpm, and the cabin should be at ambient pressure before landing [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6b]].

activities.title: True or false: decompression
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: AC 61-107B says the risk of lung damage is much lower in a rapid decompression than in an explosive one.
cards.why: True. In a rapid decompression the lungs can decompress faster than the cabin, and the risk of lung damage is significantly lower than in an explosive one [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

cards.s: In a rapid decompression, the cabin loses pressure faster than the lungs can.
cards.why: False. That describes explosive decompression. In a rapid decompression the lungs decompress faster than the cabin [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

cards.s: During an explosive decompression the ears normally clear by themselves.
cards.why: True. Normally the ears clear automatically, and air rushes from the mouth and nose [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

cards.s: Unrestricted, the lungs normally need about 2 seconds to release their air.
cards.why: False. The normal time without restrictions such as masks is 0.2 seconds [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

cards.s: Decompression from structural damage can expose occupants to wind blast and extreme cold.
cards.why: True. Structural damage also risks people near openings being tossed or blown out [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

cards.s: The pressure relief part of the safety valve opens when outside pressure is higher than cabin pressure.
cards.why: False. That is vacuum relief. Pressure relief keeps the cabin from exceeding a set differential above outside pressure [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

activities.title: Put the decompression response in order
activities.intro: One sensible generic order; your POH comes first. Use the arrows, then tap Check.
steps: Warning sounds or the cabin altimeter climbs fast: recognize the decompression
Oxygen mask on, regulator to 100 percent
Start the emergency descent: bank 30 to 45 degrees, power idle, configure per the POH
Hold airspeed under VNE, VLE, VFE (and VA in turbulence)
Call ATC: MAYDAY, the problem, your intentions
Start the recovery early and level off at a safe altitude
Land as soon as possible and get medical help for anyone with DCS signs
activities.why: Oxygen first because hypoxia is the main danger [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]; descent technique [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]; distress call [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]; DCS care [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

activities.title: FL 240, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You fly a pressurized turbocharged piston single at FL 240 on a Part 91 trip, cabin at about 8,000 ft, with three passengers you briefed on oxygen. The terrain below is flat, and you are talking to Center.

steps.s: The cabin altitude warning sounds and the cabin altimeter climbs fast. Behind you a passenger calls out that her mask is tangled.
options: Turn around and untangle her mask first, because she is the one in distress
Troubleshoot the controller and outflow valve before anything else changes
Start a descent first and put masks on below 15,000 ft once you are down there
Put your own mask on at 100 percent, then tell her neighbor to help her
steps.why: Hypoxia is the main danger and quick use of oxygen prevents unconsciousness [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Don your mask in 5 seconds or less [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]; near 25,000 ft TUC after a rapid decompression is only 1.5 to 2.5 minutes [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. Then direct the cabin while you fly (application).

steps.s: Your mask is on and oxygen is flowing. What next?
options: Climb to get above any turbulence, then wait for the cabin altitude to level off
Keep cruising and watch the gauges to see whether the cabin altitude keeps rising
Open the dump valve and stay at altitude until the cabin pressure equals the outside air
Emergency descent: bank 30 to 45 degrees, idle power, configure per the POH
steps.why: A rapid descent minimizes the problems of decompression [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]; the emergency descent uses 30 to 45 degrees of bank, idle power and the manufacturer's configuration [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

steps.s: Passing FL 200 at idle in the descent, cylinder head temperatures are dropping fast.
options: Level off at FL 200 to protect the cylinders until the engine warms up, then continue down
Climb back up to warm the engine, then make a slower descent from the higher altitude in stages
Keep descending to a safe altitude with the POH power setting; a safe altitude comes first
Shut the engine down to protect it from the cold shock and glide to a safe altitude
steps.why: A high-altitude rapid descent can cold-shock a piston engine and crack cylinders, but the top priority is reaching a safe altitude [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]]. Use the manufacturer's procedure [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

steps.s: The descent is established. Center has not heard from you.
options: Wait until you are level to avoid distraction, then call Center with the full story
MAYDAY three times, then the problem, your intentions and the help you want
Ask Center for a lower block before starting down, then report the cabin problem
Squawk nothing and switch to 121.5 only, without calling the controller on your frequency
steps.why: MAYDAY repeated three times starts a distress call; state the difficulty, intentions and assistance desired [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. In an emergency you may deviate from rules as needed [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

steps.s: Level at 10,000 ft, everyone is on oxygen and feels fine. Your destination is 90 minutes away; an airport with a hospital nearby is 20 minutes away.
options: Land at the nearby airport where medical help can be found
Continue to the destination, since everyone is on oxygen and feels fine now
Climb back to FL 240 to save fuel and time, now that the cabin problem is over
Take the masks off and continue at 10,000 ft toward the farther destination
steps.why: The AC's common procedure ends with land as soon as possible at the nearest suitable place where appropriate medical help can be found [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7e]]. DCS signs can also show up later [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
